title: Airflow, Boundary Layers and Environmental Uniformity

content.overview: Air movement affects heat exchange, humidity distribution and leaf boundary layers, but stronger airflow is not automatically better. The goal is sufficient mixing and exchange without chronic mechanical stress or isolated dead zones.

vocabulary.definition: The thin layer of relatively still air immediately surrounding a leaf surface.
A local area with poor air movement and weak exchange with the surrounding room.
Redistribution of air intended to reduce environmental gradients.

sections.title: Airflow links leaf and room conditions
sections.body: Moving air changes heat and vapor exchange around leaves and can reduce local humidity accumulation. It also changes how closely leaf conditions track room-air measurements.

sections.title: Uniformity matters more than fan count
sections.body: Several fans can still create strong jets beside stagnant interior pockets. Smoke tests, anemometer readings or repeated microclimate measurements can identify the actual distribution.

sections.title: Air movement must remain biologically tolerable
sections.body: Persistent excessive velocity can increase water demand and mechanical stress. Airflow decisions should be evaluated with leaf response, transpiration and spatial measurements.

workedExamples: If leaf edges nearest a circulation fan dry faster while interior humidity remains high, reposition or diffuse airflow instead of simply increasing fan speed.
If nighttime humidity spikes only inside dense canopy sections, investigate mixing and plant spacing along with dehumidification capacity.
commonMistakes: Equating visible leaf movement with good whole-room mixing.
Pointing strong fans continuously at one canopy area.
content.practicalApplication: Map air movement and temperature/RH at several canopy positions. Compare weak and strong zones with plant density and fan direction before changing equipment capacity.
content.summary: Useful airflow creates even exchange across the crop. Advanced control evaluates distribution, boundary-layer effects and plant response—not fan quantity alone.
